A replay attack is a form of an on-path attack, where packets are replayed at a critical time. Trojan horses are programs that enter a system or network under the guise of another program.
whyWrong: Spoofing forges an address to disrupt access, while this caller tricked a person by phone.
A replay attack resends captured packets at a critical time; it does not involve a phone call.
A Trojan horse is malware hidden in a program, not a phone call that asks for a password.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter), Volume 2 – Chapter 5: Security Concepts, Review Questions question 15

stem: You're the administrator for a large bottling company. At the end of each month, you routinely view all logs and look for discrepancies. This month, your email system error log reports a large number of unsuccessful attempts to log in. It's apparent that the email server is being targeted. Which type of attack is MOST LIKELY occurring?
explanation: A brute-force attack is a type of password attack in which a password is guessed over and over, until the right password is guessed. A backdoor attack is an embedded account that allows unauthorized access through an unpatched coding hole. A worm is different from a virus in that it can reproduce itself, is self-contained, and doesn't need a host application to be transported. A TCP/IP hijacking attempt is an attack that attempts to redirect the TCP/IP conversation to the threat agent.
whyWrong: A backdoor is a hidden way into a system and does not show as many failed logins.
A worm copies itself across the network; it does not repeatedly guess passwords.
TCP/IP hijacking takes over an existing session instead of guessing passwords.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter), Volume 2 – Chapter 5: Security Concepts, Review Questions question 18

stem: Which of the following is an attempt to guess a password by using a combination of letters and numbers?
explanation: A brute-force attack uses a combination of letters, numbers, and symbols to guess passwords, PINs, and passcodes. In contrast, a dictionary attack uses a list of words. Social engineering is an attempt to manipulate people into providing confidential information. A zero-day attack is an attack that has not yet been seen or documented, and it is very difficult to prepare for such attacks.
whyWrong: Social engineering manipulates people into giving information; it does not try character combinations.
A dictionary attack tries a list of words, not every combination of letters and numbers.
A zero-day attack exploits an unknown, unpatched vulnerability; it is not a password-guessing method.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 47: Social Engineering, Threats, and Vulnerabilities, Cram Quiz question 1

stem: A user clicked a link in an email that appeared to be from his bank. The link led him to a page that requested he change his password to access his bank account. It turns out that the web page was fraudulent. This an example of which of the following?
explanation: This is an example of phishing. Phishers use email to trick a person into divulging confidential information. While it could be said that the website that was accessed is impersonating the actual banking website, that would be more of a spoof; with true impersonation, a person mimics another person. Dumpster diving involves a person hunting through garbage or recycling to find confidential information. With shoulder surfing, a person attempts to get information by sight by, for example, looking over a person’s shoulder as that person types in a password.
whyWrong: Impersonation is a person pretending to be another person, while this attack used a fraudulent email and website.
Dumpster diving means searching trash or recycling for confidential information, not sending fraudulent emails.
Shoulder surfing means watching someone type information, not sending a fraudulent email link.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 47: Social Engineering, Threats, and Vulnerabilities, Cram Quiz question 2

stem: Several hundred infected computers simultaneously attacked your organization’s server, rendering it useless to legitimate users. This is an example of what kind of attack?
explanation: In a distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack, many computers (zombies) work together in an attempt to bring down a server or router. While it makes use of a botnet, not all botnets are necessarily bad, nor is a botnet an attack. An on-path attack is a type of spoof in which a person uses a computer to intercept and either use or change data that is captured. Tailgating is a type of social engineering attack in which a person attempts to enter a secure area by following another person without that person’s knowledge. A rainbow table is set of precalculated encrypted passwords located in a lookup table.
whyWrong: A botnet is the group of infected computers used in the attack, not the attack itself.
An on-path attack intercepts and changes data between two systems; it does not flood a server.
Tailgating is following an authorized person into a secure area, not a network attack.
A rainbow table is a lookup table of precalculated password hashes, not a flood of traffic.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 47: Social Engineering, Threats, and Vulnerabilities, Cram Quiz question 3

stem: A hacker executed a coded attack against a vulnerability that has not yet been addressed by anyone. This is an example of what kind of attack?
explanation: A zero-day attack is an attack that exploits vulnerabilities that have not yet been discovered (besides by the attacker, that is). A DDoS attack is an attack that incorporates many systems in a collective attack against a server or network device. A spoofing attack involves technical impersonation; for example, a computer system sitting between a client and a server may impersonate the server in an attempt to retrieve user data. A brute-force attack is a password-based attack in which every conceivable password is attempted.
whyWrong: A DDoS attack uses many systems to flood a target; it does not depend on an unknown vulnerability.
A spoofing attack impersonates another system; the key point here is an unaddressed vulnerability.
A brute-force attack guesses every possible password; it does not exploit an unknown flaw.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 47: Social Engineering, Threats, and Vulnerabilities, Cram Quiz question 4

stem: What is the primary method used in vishing to deceive individuals?
options: Making phone calls with automated messages
explanation: Vishing is initiated via a phone call, often using an automated VoIP system or home-brewed private branch exchange (PBX). These calls frequently use prerecorded messages to mimic legitimate institutions. Sending fraudulent emails is the method used in standard phishing, not vishing. Distributing infected software, while a cyber threat, is not the core method of vishing. Creating fake websites is also a method of standard phishing, not vishing.
whyWrong: Fraudulent emails are the method of standard phishing, not vishing.
Distributing infected software is a malware threat, not the core method of vishing.
Fake websites are a method of standard phishing, not of vishing, which uses phone calls.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 47: Social Engineering, Threats, and Vulnerabilities, Cram Quiz question 5

stem: What is the primary function of an evil twin in a wireless network attack?
options: To distribute malicious software through email attachments
To impersonate a legitimate access point and capture user data
To manipulate employee behavior through social engineering tactics
explanation: An evil twin is a rogue, counterfeit, and unauthorized wireless access point that uses the same SSID name as a nearby wireless network to gain valuable information and passwords from those users. Distributing malicious software through email attachments describes a Trojan horse, for example, not an evil twin. Physically damaging network hardware is not the main purpose of an evil twin attack. While social engineering can be used in conjunction with an evil twin, the core function is the impersonation of a wireless access point, not direct social manipulation.
whyWrong: Malicious email attachments describe a Trojan horse, not an evil twin access point.
An evil twin does not physically damage hardware; it imitates a wireless network.
Social engineering may be used with it, but the core of an evil twin is a fake access point.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 47: Social Engineering, Threats, and Vulnerabilities, Cram Quiz question 6

stem: Why is a computer that runs an operating system past its end-of-life (EOL) date a security vulnerability?
options: The vendor no longer releases security patches for it
The operating system stops booting after the EOL date
Its license key is revoked and it cannot join a network
Its built-in firewall is removed by the vendor
explanation: When an operating system reaches its end of life, the vendor stops supplying security updates for it. New vulnerabilities found after that date stay unfixed. The system then puts the whole network at risk, so it should be upgraded to a supported version.
whyWrong: An EOL operating system still boots and runs; the problem is that it no longer gets fixes.
EOL does not revoke the license or block network access; the system keeps working without patches.
The vendor does not remove features such as the firewall; it only stops releasing updates.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 47: Social Engineering, Threats, and Vulnerabilities

stem: Company policy says every workstation must get the monthly OS updates and current antimalware definitions. A network scan finds one PC that skipped several months of updates and still runs old definitions. Which vulnerability term BEST describes this PC?
explanation: A non-compliant system is one that does not meet the organization's security policy, such as its update rules. Because the PC sits inside the firewall with the other computers, an attacker could use it to reach systems that are up to date. Scanning the network finds such systems so they can be brought back into compliance.
whyWrong: A zero-day attack exploits a flaw that has no patch yet, but patches for this PC exist and were skipped.
An evil twin is a rogue wireless access point that copies a real SSID, not an outdated PC.
An insider threat is a person inside the organization who causes harm, not a missed update.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 47: Social Engineering, Threats, and Vulnerabilities

stem: During an audit, a technician finds a file server with no antivirus software installed and its firewall turned off. Its OS updates are current. Which vulnerability does this server show?
explanation: An unprotected system is one that is missing antivirus or firewall protection. Without antivirus, the server can catch malware and spread it to other computers. Without a firewall, unauthorized connections can reach services and exploit any weakness in the OS.
whyWrong: An EOL system no longer receives vendor updates, but this server is current on its OS updates.
BYOD refers to personal devices that employees bring to work, not a company file server.
A supply chain attack compromises a vendor or product before delivery; it is a threat, not a missing protection.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter) – Core 2 Chapter 5: Security Concepts

stem: A chief information officer (CIO) receives an email from the chief executive officer (CEO) requesting confidential information to be supplied. The email appears to originate from a personal email address that the CIO does not recognize. What type of attack is this likely to be?
explanation: When a single individual is targeted and that individual has a senior management position, they are considered a big fish. So, whaling is based on phishing, but it is a targeted attack against the big fish (a user in a senior position).
whyWrong: Phishing is a broad attack on many users, while this one targets a single senior executive.
Dumpster diving means searching trash for useful documents, not sending a fake email.
Shoulder surfing means watching someone type a password or PIN, not sending an email.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 8: Security, Objective 2.4 question 1

stem: A user is picking up printed documents from the centralized office printer. Despite the large number of other users in the crowded print room, after a wait in line, the user is able to successfully type in their password to pull down the print job. Later, the user is warned of a suspicious login using the same credentials. What social engineering event likely took place?
explanation: Shoulder surfing is likely to take place in congested spaces when an attacker can be in close proximity to observe a user typing a password. A crowded print room gives the attacker a chance to watch the password being entered.
whyWrong: Phishing uses messages with links to trick users, not watching someone type a password.
Vishing gets information through a voice call, not by watching a user at a printer.
Whaling is phishing aimed at senior executives and uses email rather than observation.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 8: Security, Objective 2.4 question 2

stem: A team of contractors arrives on site, wearing shirts and jackets with the logo of a well-known support contractor. The contractors say they are responding to error messages that have been received from the bank’s critical servers in the data center. There is no record of a support call being generated. What is the likely vector of attack?
explanation: As the contractors have turned up unannounced, this could represent a threat. In this case, they are using impersonation by wearing clothing that gives them the appearance of genuine support contractors.
whyWrong: Tailgating means following a valid user closely through a controlled door, not posing as a contractor.
Dumpster diving means stealing documents from the trash, which is not happening here.
An evil twin is a malicious Wi-Fi access point, not people arriving on site in disguise.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 8: Security, Objective 2.4 question 3

stem: A user raises a support ticket complaining about slow Wi-Fi speeds, local mapped drives, and printers not being available. On several occasions, the user has been asked for credentials when connected to internet sites. The user suspects that their online accounts may have been compromised. What is the likely threat vector?
explanation: An evil twin refers to a deceptive and malicious wireless network that is designed to resemble a legitimate network. It is essentially a rogue access point that appears to be a trusted Wi-Fi network but is set up by an attacker with the intention of intercepting sensitive information or conducting other malicious activities. As the access point is not connected to a legitimate trusted network, mapped drives and shared printers will not be accessible.
whyWrong: Tailgating is following someone through a secure door and does not affect Wi-Fi or mapped drives.
Impersonation means posing as a trusted person, which does not explain the missing drives and printers.
Dumpster diving means searching the trash for information and has no effect on network access.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 8: Security, Objective 2.4 question 4

stem: A courier wearing a high-visibility jacket carrying a parcel follows an employee into an unmanned reception area. Later, it is discovered that laptop computers and a tablet have been reported as missing or stolen. What was the likely cause of this security breach?
explanation: Tailgating is when an unauthorized person pretends to be an employee, delivery person, or visitor and attempts to enter a secure area by closely following an authorized employee through a controlled access point, such as a door with an access card or a security checkpoint. Here the courier followed an employee in and later stole the devices.
whyWrong: Impersonation is posing as someone trusted; the key act here is following an employee through the door.
Dumpster diving means searching the trash for documents, not walking into the building.
An evil twin is a rogue wireless access point and does not involve entering a building.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 8: Security, Objective 2.4 question 5

stem: An online retailer receives multiple complaints that customers cannot access the site. Upon investigation, engineers discover thousands of remote connections to the site’s web servers. The connections do not appear to be genuine customers logging in to the site. What is the likely threat?
explanation: In a DDoS attack, the targeted network or system becomes overloaded and is unable to handle legitimate user requests, effectively denying service to legitimate users. DDoS attacks can involve thousands of connections. Botnets can be used to generate massive amounts of traffic.
whyWrong: A DoS attack can come from a single host and does not involve thousands of remote connections.
A zero-day attack exploits a flaw with no patch available, not a flood of connections.
Spoofing fakes the email, IP, or MAC address of a genuine host rather than flooding a site.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 8: Security, Objective 2.4 question 6

stem: A user is attempting to log in to their online banking site, but the web browser reports an error regarding the website certificate. The URL in the browser does not appear to be the normal URL that the user was expecting. What type of attack is likely occurring?
explanation: An on-path attack refers to a type of network attack where an adversary gains control or inserts themselves into the communication path between two networked entities. This enables them to intercept, modify, or block network traffic flowing between these entities, allowing them to eavesdrop on sensitive information, manipulate data, or disrupt communication. This type of attack is also known as man in the middle (MiTM).
whyWrong: An insider threat is a malicious or careless employee and does not explain a certificate error on the site.
SQL injection targets the database behind a web application, not the user’s connection to the bank.
Cross-site scripting injects scripts into a web application and does not change the URL and certificate.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 8: Security, Objective 2.4 question 7

stem:
A security engineer is investigating logs on the customer-facing web application server. One of the entries is causing the engineer concern. The following string is logged: <script>alert('http://malwaresite.com/javascriptcookiestealer.com')</script>

What type of attack has likely occurred?
explanation: The main goal of an XSS attack is to manipulate the website’s content and interact with the user’s session. If the script can be uploaded to the web server, then other users will automatically run the script when they use a browser to visit the site. The malicious payload is identified by the use of arrowhead brackets, <>.
whyWrong: Spoofing fakes a network identity and does not insert script tags into a web application.
SQL injection uses database query syntax, not HTML script tags like those in the log.
A zero-day attack describes a flaw with no patch, not a specific script payload in a log.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 8: Security, Objective 2.4 question 8

stem: An attacker is able to target a vulnerability present on a web server where there is no available patch or update. What type of threat does this describe?
explanation: A zero-day attack is used to describe a vulnerability where there is no patch available. The attacker uses the flaw before the vendor can release a fix.
whyWrong: An insider threat comes from someone inside the organization, not from an unpatched web server flaw.
SQL injection manipulates database queries and is not defined by the lack of a patch.
Cross-site scripting injects scripts into web pages and is not defined by the lack of a patch.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 8: Security, Objective 2.4 question 9

stem:
An attacker is able to log on to a website, despite the fact that the attacker has not been assigned valid credentials. The logs indicate that the attacker was able to access the site using the first account stored in a table on the database server. The following log entry was recorded around the time of the incident: SELECT * FROM Users WHERE Username=foo' OR '1' = '1' AND Password='pass' OR '1' = '1'

What type of attack has occurred?
explanation: In a SQL injection attack, attackers exploit vulnerabilities in a web application’s input fields to manipulate the SQL queries executed by the application’s database. In this case, the attacker has entered a malicious input into the login fields that alters the SQL query executed by the application. The condition ‘1’ = ‘1’ is always true, so the attacker is essentially bypassing the authentication process by manipulating the query to return results for any username and password combination.
whyWrong: A brute-force attack tries many password combinations, and the log shows no repeated attempts.
A dictionary attack tries common words as passwords, which does not match this altered query.
Cross-site scripting injects scripts that other users run and does not alter database queries.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 8: Security, Objective 2.4 question 10

stem: During a security awareness briefing, users are given examples of password attacks. Which of the following is a common method for “brute-forcing” passwords?
options: Repeatedly trying different combinations of characters
explanation: A brute-force password attack is a technique used by hackers to gain unauthorized access to a system or account by systematically trying all possible combinations of passwords until the correct one is found. It is a straightforward and exhaustive method where the attacker uses automated tools to generate and try different passwords in rapid succession.
whyWrong: Guessing common passwords or phrases from a word list is a dictionary attack.
Exploiting software vulnerabilities is not a password attack method.
Intercepting network traffic is packet sniffing, which may capture passwords but is not brute force.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 8: Security, Objective 2.6 question 7

stem: Edna wants to put a policy in place at her company to prevent or at least limit viruses. What policies would offer the BEST solution?
options: Install antivirus software on every computer. Teach users how to run it.
Install antivirus software on every computer. Set up the software to scan regularly.
Install antivirus software on every computer. Set up the software to update the definitions and engine automatically. Set up the software to scan regularly.

Install antivirus software on every computer. Set up the software to update the definitions and engine automatically. Set up the software to scan regularly. Educate the users about sites and downloads to avoid.
explanation: The best policy includes updating the software engine and definitions, scanning PCs regularly, and educating users. Educating users is the last step of the malware removal procedure because many infections start with a user action.
whyWrong: Without updates and scheduled scans, the software misses new threats.
Regular scans with old definitions will not detect new viruses.
This leaves out user education, which prevents many infections.
source: CompTIA A+ Certification All-in-One Exam Guide, 11th ed. – Chapter 27: Securing Computers, Chapter Review question 10
note: 220-1102 3.3; mapped to 220-1202 2.6 (schedule scans and run updates, educate the end user).

stem: A computer has been infected with multiple viruses and spyware. Which of the following tasks should be performed before removing this malware?
explanation: For proper quarantining and removal of malware, you usually have to disable System Restore first because it can get in the way of the antimalware scanning and removal processes by possibly reinfecting the computer. Restore points can hold copies of the malware, so they could reinfect the computer if they stay enabled.
whyWrong: Disabling the network card in Windows may not work if malware controls the system; disconnect it physically instead.
Windows Update is run after the malware is quarantined and removed.
chkdsk /R finds bad sectors, which may be done after the malware removal, not before.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – A+ Core 2 (220-1202) Practice Exam, Practice Exam question 73

stem: According to the 10 steps to remove malware from a SOHO environment, which of the following actions is recommended after the malware has been removed from a system?
options: Boot into Safe Mode/preinstallation environment to limit malware activity.
explanation: In step 8, after removing the malware, it is suggested to schedule regular full system scans with your antivirus software. Also, keep your operating system, applications, and browser extensions updated to patch vulnerabilities and prevent future infections.
whyWrong: Booting into Safe Mode is part of the removal process, not a step after it.
Reimaging is done during removal when other methods fail, not after a successful removal.
Quarantining is step 2, one of the first steps, not a step after removal.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – A+ Core 2 (220-1202) Practice Exam, Practice Exam question 89

stem: After performing a System Restore on a Windows workstation that was affected by malware, the technician notices that the malware is still detected. Which of the following BEST explains why the system still has malware?
options: The antivirus protection and host firewall were disabled by a system patch
The system updates did not include the latest anti-malware definitions
The malware compromised the System Restore process
The malware was installed before the creation of the System Restore point
explanation: System Restore returns system files, settings, and the registry to the state saved in a restore point. If the malware was already on the system when that restore point was made, restoring to it brings the malware back. This is why System Restore is disabled during malware removal, and a new restore point is made only after the system is clean.
whyWrong: A patch disabling protection would not explain why the malware survived a restore.
Missing definitions do not explain why the restore did not remove the malware.
Malware does not need to compromise System Restore to survive; a restore point made after the infection already contains it.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 11: Mock Exam: Core 2 (220-1102), Mock Exam question 61
note: 220-1102 3.3; mapped to 220-1202 2.6 (disable System Restore). Book answer C (the malware compromised System Restore) corrected: the usual reason is that the restore point was made after the infection and keeps the malware, which is why the removal steps disable System Restore.

stem: A computer on a corporate network has been infected with malware. What is the most effective method for restoring the computer to operational status?
options: Scanning the system with a Linux live disk, flashing the BIOS, and then returning the computer to service
Flashing the BIOS, reformatting the drive, and then reinstalling the OS
Degaussing the hard drive, flashing the BIOS, and then reinstalling the OS
Reinstalling the OS, flashing the BIOS, and then scanning with on-premises antivirus
explanation: The best method for returning the computer to service after a malware infection is to first reinstall the OS to ensure a clean and fresh installation, removing any traces of the malware. Next, flashing the BIOS is recommended to restore the firmware to its original state, removing any malware that may have infected the BIOS. Finally, scanning the computer with on-premises antivirus software will help identify and eliminate any remaining malware threats, providing an additional layer of protection.
whyWrong: A Linux live scan followed by a BIOS flash does not remove the infected OS.
Reformatting without the book's reinstall-and-scan order leaves the computer without a clean, checked OS.
Degaussing is for destroying data on magnetic media, not for removing malware.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 11: Mock Exam: Core 2 (220-1102), Mock Exam question 67
note: 220-1102 3.3; mapped to 220-1202 2.6 (reimage/reinstall). The book's order of steps is kept.

stem:
You are a technician for an accounting company. You are helping a user who is unable to access websites and is reporting connectivity issues as well as pop-ups on the screen. You discover and remove malware. After rebooting the system, you are able to ping the gateway and access the Internet.

Which of the following NEXT steps should you take while troubleshooting this issue? (Select the two best answers.)
options: Reboot the computer and verify that it works.
Research the problem based on the symptoms you found.
Reconnect the system to the network.
explanation: You should perform a virus scan and then document findings, actions, and outcomes. A follow-up scan confirms that no malware is left after the removal. Documentation is the final step of the troubleshooting process.
whyWrong: The computer was already rebooted in the scenario, so rebooting again adds nothing.
The problem is already found and fixed, so there is nothing left to research.
Pinging the gateway and reaching the Internet already show the TCP/IP settings are fine.
The system already reaches the Internet, so it is clearly reconnected to the network.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – A+ Core 1 (220-1201) Practice Exam, Practice Exam question 6
note: From the Core 1 practice exam; the malware removal steps are 220-1202 2.6. Documenting the findings is the last step of the troubleshooting method.

stem: In Windows, which utility is responsible for finding, downloading, and installing Windows patches?
explanation: Windows Update is responsible for downloading and installing Windows service packs, patches, and security updates. Device Manager is used to view devices installed on the operating system. The Microsoft Management Console is a console that allows snap-ins to be added for management. Download Manager is a component of Edge.
whyWrong: Device Manager shows and manages installed hardware; it does not download patches.
The Microsoft Management Console hosts snap-ins for management; it does not install Windows patches.
Download Manager is a part of the Edge browser that tracks downloaded files, not Windows patches.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter), Volume 2 – Chapter 7: Troubleshooting Operating Systems and Security, Review Questions question 1
note: Windows Update is in 220-1202 1.6 (Update and Security); mapped to 220-1202 2.6.8 (run updates).

stem: What is the FIRST step in malware removal?
options: Identify and verify the malware symptoms.
explanation: The most important first step is to identify and verify the malware symptoms. You should quarantine the infected system once you have verified it is infected. Remediating the infected system happens after you disable System Restore. Education of the end user is the last step to malware removal.
whyWrong: Quarantine comes after the infection is confirmed, so it is the second step.
Remediation happens after the system is quarantined and System Restore is disabled.
Educating the end user is the last step of malware removal, not the first.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter), Volume 2 – Chapter 7: Troubleshooting Operating Systems and Security, Review Questions question 4

stem: In general, how often should you update your antivirus definitions?
options: Antivirus definitions do not need to be updated.
explanation: Antivirus definitions should be updated daily, because new viruses are identified by the minute. Updating antivirus definitions weekly or monthly will open you up to the possibility of infection. Most antivirus software can check for new definitions automatically.
whyWrong: Weekly updates leave days in which new viruses are not detected.
Monthly updates leave weeks in which new viruses are not detected.
Antivirus software can detect only the viruses that its definitions describe, so updates are needed.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter), Volume 2 – Chapter 7: Troubleshooting Operating Systems and Security, Review Questions question 10

stem: Why is it important to disable System Restore in Windows Home during malware removal?
options: It speeds up the scanning process.
It prevents malware from being restored from a backup.
It frees up disk space for the antimalware software to operate.
It forces the malware to become active, making it easier to detect.
explanation: Disabling System Restore during malware removal prevents malware from being restored from a backup. System Restore points can inadvertently contain malware. Disabling System Restore prevents the malware from being reintroduced during the recovery process. Disabling System Restore doesn’t necessarily speed up the scanning, nor does it directly affect free disk space. Malware doesn’t need to be active to be detected.
whyWrong: Disabling System Restore does not speed up the antimalware scan.
Disabling System Restore is not about freeing disk space for the antimalware software.
Malware does not need to be active to be detected, and disabling System Restore does not activate it.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 51: SOHO Security, Cram Quiz 1 question 1

stem: Which of the following is the most drastic step in malware removal but also ensures a completely clean system?
options: Running a full system scan in Safe Mode
Using a dedicated malware removal tool
Reimaging or reinstalling the operating system
explanation: The most drastic step in malware removal is reimaging or reinstalling the operating system. Doing so completely wipes the hard drive and installs a fresh copy of Windows, eliminating any deeply embedded malware. Safe Mode scans are helpful but might not remove all malware, and dedicated tools are useful but not always guaranteed to remove everything. Disabling startup programs might not address the root cause of the infection.
whyWrong: A full scan in Safe Mode helps, but it might not remove all malware.
A dedicated malware removal tool is useful but is not guaranteed to remove everything.
Disabling suspicious startup programs might not remove the root cause of the infection.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 51: SOHO Security, Cram Quiz 1 question 2
note: Option A fixed from the book's typo "full system can" to "full system scan".

stem: A technician has quarantined an infected Windows Home PC and disabled System Restore. When the technician starts to remediate the system, what should be done FIRST?
options: Update the anti-malware software and its definitions
Reimage the drive and reinstall Windows
Enable System Restore and create a restore point
Teach the user how the infection happened
explanation: Remediation starts by updating the anti-malware software so it has the latest definitions. Current definitions give the scan the best chance of finding and removing the malware. Scans in Safe Mode or a preinstallation environment come after that, and reimaging is a last resort.
whyWrong: Reimaging is the last resort of remediation, used only when scanning and removal do not work.
Enabling System Restore and creating a restore point comes after the system is clean.
Educating the user is the final step of the procedure, after the system is clean.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 51: SOHO Security

stem: A technician has removed malware from a Windows Home PC, scheduled regular scans, and run all updates. What should the technician do NEXT?
options: Enable System Restore and create a new restore point
Disable System Restore and delete the old restore points
Disconnect the PC from the network to quarantine it
Update the anti-malware definitions and scan in Safe Mode
explanation: After scans are scheduled and updates are run, the procedure turns System Restore back on and creates a restore point. That restore point records a clean state the PC can return to later. Educating the end user is the only step left after that.
whyWrong: Disabling System Restore happens early in the procedure, before remediation, not after the system is clean.
Quarantine is the second step of the procedure and was needed before the malware was removed.
Updating definitions and scanning are part of remediation, which this technician has already finished.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 51: SOHO Security

stem: Why does the malware removal procedure end with creating a new restore point after the system is clean?
options: It gives a clean, known-good state to roll back to later
It removes any malware that is still in memory
It updates the anti-malware definitions automatically
It encrypts the user's files against ransomware
explanation: The old restore points were deleted or may contain the infection, so the PC has no safe point to return to. A new restore point made after cleaning records a known-good state. If a later change or problem occurs, the system can roll back to it without bringing the malware back.
whyWrong: A restore point only saves system settings and files; it does not scan for or remove malware.
Definitions are updated by the anti-malware program or Windows Update, not by creating a restore point.
Restore points do not encrypt files; protection against ransomware comes from backups and anti-malware tools.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter) – Core 2 Chapter 7: Troubleshooting Operating Systems and Security

stem: In Windows 11, where does a technician turn System Protection back on for the C: drive and then select Create to make a restore point?
options: The System Protection tab of System Properties
Settings, then Windows Update, then Advanced options
explanation: System Restore is set up in the System Protection tab of System Properties. A technician can reach it from Control Panel, then Recovery, then Configure System Restore, or by searching for Create a restore point. There the technician selects the system drive, clicks Configure to turn on protection, and then clicks Create.
whyWrong: Windows Update settings control how updates install; they do not turn on System Protection.
Task Scheduler runs tasks on a schedule, such as scans, but it is not where protection is turned on.
Disk Management manages partitions and volumes and has no restore point settings.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter) – Core 2 Chapter 7: Troubleshooting Operating Systems and Security

stem: After installing a new video driver from an unofficial third-party internet site, a user’s workstation is exhibiting strange behavior. The workstation is running slowly, and the user reports no other changes have been made apart from the updated driver. What action will allow a technician to BEST determine whether the driver is the cause of the behavior?
options: Reboot the workstation into recovery mode, select Troubleshoot\Advanced options\Startup settings, and choose to enable Safe Mode
Configure Windows Firewall to block all outgoing connections
explanation: Windows Safe Mode will allow the system to be launched using a minimal set of drivers. If the newly installed video driver is corrupt or malfunctioning, then Safe Mode should launch into a stable desktop environment.
whyWrong: An anti-virus scan may find malicious code but cannot show whether the driver is corrupt or incompatible.
Updating anti-malware helps detection but does not test whether the new driver causes the problem.
Blocking outgoing connections in the firewall does not show whether the driver is stable.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 8: Security, Objective 2.3 question 10
note: 220-1102 2.3; mapped to 220-1202 2.6 (scan and removal techniques, safe mode).

stem: A technician has quarantined a user’s Windows 10 laptop after an unknown process was found running on the system. The process is identified as malicious and is documented on many anti-virus vendor sites. The user has been using the laptop on a network with no internet access for 2 months. What should the technician do NEXT?
options: Update Windows Defender definition files and run a full anti-virus scan
Manually remove the malicious file and return the laptop to the user
Use a system restore to revert to the last restore point
Wipe the system and perform a fresh Windows installation
explanation: It is important to ensure all security updates and anti-virus definitions are kept up to date. In this case, the system was not able to be kept up to date, so the best action is to pull down all updates and then run a full scan.
whyWrong: Removing one file by hand may leave other undetected malware on the laptop.
Restoring a restore point can reinfect the system; restore points are deleted during malware removal.
Wiping and reinstalling Windows is a last resort after other remediation steps have failed.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 8: Security, Objective 2.5 question 7
note: 220-1102 2.5; mapped to 220-1202 2.6 (malware removal: update anti-malware software).

stem: A user’s computer is exhibiting slow performance, frequent pop-up advertisements, and unexpected system restarts. Upon investigation, you suspect the presence of malware. What is the BEST practice procedure to remove the malware from the computer?
options: Disconnect the computer from the network, perform a full system scan using updated anti-malware software, and remove any detected malware
Manually delete suspicious files and folders from the computer, then restart it to check for any further issues
Re-install the operating system to ensure the complete removal of all malware
Ignore the issue as it may be a temporary glitch in the system
explanation: The best practice procedure for malware removal in this scenario is to disconnect the computer from the network to prevent further infection, perform a full system scan using updated anti-malware software to detect any malware, and then remove any detected malware. This approach ensures the thorough removal of the malicious software and helps restore the system’s performance and stability.
whyWrong: Deleting files by hand misses hidden and system-level malware, so the infection can remain.
Reinstalling the OS is a last resort for when removal tools fail or the system is badly compromised.
Ignoring the symptoms lets the malware cause more damage, data loss, and security breaches.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 9: Software Troubleshooting, Objective 3.3 question 1
note: 220-1102 3.3; mapped to 220-1202 2.6 (malware removal procedure in the old objectives).

stem: Which of the following is the recommended practice for updating anti-malware software?
options: Disable automatic updates to prevent interruption during important tasks
Update the software manually only when prompted by the operating system
Configure the software to update automatically and regularly
Uninstall and re-install the software to ensure the latest version is installed
explanation: The recommended practice for updating anti-malware software is to configure it to update automatically and regularly. This ensures that the software receives the latest virus definitions, security patches, and feature updates, providing the most effective protection against new and emerging threats.
whyWrong: Turning off updates leaves the software without the newest definitions, so new threats are missed.
Waiting for an OS prompt delays critical definition updates and leaves the system exposed.
A reinstall is not needed because anti-malware software updates itself from inside the application.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 9: Software Troubleshooting, Objective 3.3 question 2
note: 220-1102 3.3; mapped to 220-1202 2.6 (malware removal procedure in the old objectives).

stem: Why is it important to investigate and verify malware symptoms before proceeding with the removal process?
options: It helps to determine the cost of the malware removal process
It allows for more accurate identification and selection of appropriate removal techniques.
It helps in estimating the time required to remove the malware
It ensures the end user is educated about the potential risks of malware
explanation: It is important to investigate and verify malware symptoms before proceeding with the removal process because it allows for more accurate identification and selection of appropriate removal techniques. Different types of malware may exhibit different symptoms, and understanding these symptoms helps in determining the most effective course of action.
whyWrong: Checking symptoms is about choosing the right removal method, not about working out the cost.
Removal time depends on many factors, so estimating it is not the purpose of checking symptoms.
End-user education is a later step of the procedure and is not why symptoms are verified first.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 9: Software Troubleshooting, Objective 3.3 question 3
note: 220-1102 3.3; mapped to 220-1202 2.6 (malware removal procedure in the old objectives).

stem: A technician must follow best practice procedures to BEST prevent future malware infections. Which best practice should be followed?
options: Disable the system’s user account control (UAC) feature
Share user credentials with trusted colleagues
Enable all browser extensions and plugins by default
explanation: Regularly updating anti-virus software is crucial for staying protected against new malware threats. Updates often include the latest virus definitions, improved detection algorithms, and security enhancements, ensuring the anti-virus software can effectively identify and remove the latest malware variants.
whyWrong: Turning off UAC removes a defense against unauthorized changes and makes infection easier.
Sharing credentials allows unauthorized access and raises the risk of infection.
Enabling every extension and plug-in widens the attack surface for malware.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 9: Software Troubleshooting, Objective 3.3 question 4
note: 220-1102 3.3; mapped to 220-1202 2.6 (malware removal procedure in the old objectives).

stem: Why is it necessary to quarantine infected systems during the malware removal process?
options: To prevent the malware from spreading to other systems
To disable System Restore in Windows
To create a restore point for future use
To schedule scans and run updates
explanation: Quarantining infected systems is necessary during the malware removal process to prevent the malware from spreading to other systems. By isolating the infected systems, the risk of further contamination is minimized, protecting other devices on the network.
whyWrong: System Restore is disabled in a separate step of the procedure, not by quarantining the system.
A new restore point is created at the end of the procedure after the system is clean.
Scans and updates are separate steps that happen after the system is isolated.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 9: Software Troubleshooting, Objective 3.3 question 5
note: 220-1102 3.3; mapped to 220-1202 2.6 (malware removal procedure in the old objectives).

stem: What is the purpose of disabling System Restore in Windows during malware removal?
options: To prevent the malware from spreading to other systems
To remove any infected restore points
To ensure the malware cannot re-infect the system after removal
To speed up the malware removal process
explanation: Disabling System Restore in Windows during malware removal is done primarily to remove any infected restore points. Malware can hide in these restore points, allowing it to survive even after the malware removal process. By disabling System Restore, all existing restore points are deleted, reducing the chances of the malware reappearing.
whyWrong: Isolating the system from the network is what stops malware from spreading to other computers.
Disabling System Restore alone cannot stop a new infection after the malware is removed.
Disabling System Restore removes infected restore points; it does not make the scan faster.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 9: Software Troubleshooting, Objective 3.3 question 6
note: 220-1102 3.3; mapped to 220-1202 2.6 (malware removal procedure in the old objectives).

stem: What happens when System Restore is disabled during malware removal?
options: The malware is immediately deleted from the system
All existing restore points are deleted
The malware is isolated and prevented from executing
The system becomes immune to further malware infections
explanation: When System Restore is disabled during malware removal, all existing restore points are deleted. This action helps remove any potential hiding places for the malware, making it harder for it to survive and re-infect the system. Disabling System Restore does not immediately delete the malware from the system.
whyWrong: Turning off System Restore deletes restore points but leaves the active malware for the scanner to remove.
Turning off System Restore does not isolate the malware or stop it from running.
No step makes a system immune; other security measures are still needed after removal.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 9: Software Troubleshooting, Objective 3.3 question 7
note: 220-1102 3.3; mapped to 220-1202 2.6 (malware removal procedure in the old objectives).

stem: Why is it important to educate the end user as part of the malware removal process?
options: To shift the responsibility of malware removal to the end user
To enhance the end user’s technical skills
To minimize the risk of re-infection and prevent future malware incidents
To create a sense of panic and urgency among end users
explanation: Educating the end user is crucial in reducing the likelihood of future malware incidents. By teaching the end user about safe browsing habits, recognizing phishing attempts, and avoiding suspicious downloads, they become more aware of potential threats and are less likely to fall victim to malware. This helps minimize the risk of re-infection.
whyWrong: Education is shared work with IT staff and does not hand malware removal over to the user.
Better technical skills may be a side effect, but the main goal is to prevent another infection.
Creating panic is counterproductive; education should give users the knowledge to avoid threats.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 9: Software Troubleshooting, Objective 3.3 question 8
note: 220-1102 3.3; mapped to 220-1202 2.6 (malware removal procedure in the old objectives).

stem: Which of the following is a potential benefit of educating the end user about malware removal?
explanation: Educating the end user about malware removal can lead to faster incident response times. When end users are aware of potential malware threats and know how to report suspicious activities promptly, IT professionals can respond quickly and mitigate the impact of the incident.
whyWrong: Trained users stay productive because they avoid infections and report problems sooner.
Education aims to reduce, not increase, the user's need for IT support.
Trained users are less likely, not more likely, to cause a data breach.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 9: Software Troubleshooting, Objective 3.3 question 9
note: 220-1102 3.3; mapped to 220-1202 2.6 (malware removal procedure in the old objectives).

stem: What is one potential consequence of neglecting to educate the end user about malware removal?
options: Higher incidence of successful malware attacks
explanation: Neglecting to educate the end user about malware removal can lead to a higher incidence of successful malware attacks. If end users are not aware of safe practices and do not know how to identify and report potential threats, they become more vulnerable to malware attacks.
whyWrong: Skipping education does not directly raise the IT budget, and more budget would not fix the cause.
Slow performance comes from the malware itself, not directly from a lack of user education.
Lost bandwidth is caused by malware activity, not directly by the missing user education.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 9: Software Troubleshooting, Objective 3.3 question 10
note: 220-1102 3.3; mapped to 220-1202 2.6 (malware removal procedure in the old objectives).

stem: Dana, a technician, confirms that a home user's Windows 11 Home laptop has spyware and unplugs it from the network. What should Dana do NEXT?
options: Run a full scan in Safe Mode
Explain to the user how the spyware got in
explanation: After the symptoms are verified and the system is quarantined, System Restore is disabled. This keeps the malware from being saved in or restored from a restore point during the cleanup.
whyWrong: The scan is part of remediation, which comes only after System Restore is disabled.
A new restore point is made only after the system is clean, near the end of the procedure.
Educating the user is the final step, after the system is clean and protected.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 51: SOHO Security

stem: A small-office PC is quarantined and its anti-malware definitions are current, but the malware closes the scanner each time it starts inside Windows. Which approach is BEST for the technician to try?
options: Scan the PC in Safe Mode
Schedule a weekly scan in Task Scheduler
explanation: Safe Mode loads only basic drivers and services, so most malware does not start and cannot stop the scanner. If that fails, an offline scan from a preinstallation environment is the next choice.
whyWrong: Reinstalling is the last resort of remediation and is used only after the scan and removal methods fail.
System Restore stays off until the system is clean, so the infection is not saved in a restore point.
Scheduling scans protects the PC after removal; it does not get past malware that stops the scanner.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 51: SOHO Security

stem: At a retail store, a kiosk PC's files are encrypted by ransomware. Safe Mode and offline scans could not remove the malware, and the kiosk's data is in a clean backup. What is the BEST way to remediate the kiosk?
options: Reimage the drive, then restore the data from the backup
Pay the ransom to get the decryption key
Roll the PC back with System Restore
Run the same offline scan again
explanation: When removal tools fail, reimaging or reinstalling is the last-resort remediation step. Ransomware usually cannot be undone, so the malware is removed and the user data is restored from a backup.
whyWrong: Paying gives no guarantee that the files come back and is not part of the removal procedure.
System Restore is disabled during malware removal, and ransomware often deletes the restore points anyway.
The offline scan has already failed, so running it again will not clean the kiosk.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter) – Core 2 Chapter 7: Troubleshooting Operating Systems and Security

stem: To make your files unreadable by others, what should you use?
explanation: To make your files unreadable by others, use encryption. Encrypted data can be read only by someone who has the key, such as with EFS or BitLocker in Windows.
whyWrong: Clustering groups disk sectors into allocation units; it does not hide data from others.
Compression makes files smaller, but anyone with access can still read them.
Disk quotas limit how much space a user may use; they do not make files unreadable.
source: CompTIA A+ Certification All-in-One Exam Guide, 11th ed. – Chapter 9: Implementing Mass Storage, Chapter Review question 6

stem: One of the users in your company frequently leaves their workstation and wants to make sure that their confidential data is not accessed by anyone else. However, the user does not want to turn off the computer when they leave work in the evening. Which of the following is the BEST solution for securing the workstation?
options: Implement a password and fingerprint lock for after-hours login.
Set a strong password that requires a renewal every 30 days.
Apply a screen lock after 5 minutes of nonuse and set login time restrictions for after-hours.
Run a screensaver after 1 minute of nonuse and a fingerprint lock for after-hours.
explanation: The screen lock and login time restrictions are your best bet. This way, the computer will lock after 5 minutes, even if the user forgets to lock it manually (with a quick Windows+L on the keyboard). Set the login restriction hours within the system or on the domain so that no one can log in after a certain time (such as 5 p.m.).
whyWrong: A fingerprint lock only for after-hours does nothing when the user walks away during the day.
A strong password with renewal does not lock the computer when the user leaves it.
A screensaver does not necessarily require a password to unlock it.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – A+ Core 2 (220-1202) Practice Exam, Practice Exam question 12

stem: You are an end-user technician working for a computer support company. A typical customer says that they are concerned about the privacy of their home laptop and the security of the network in general when browsing the Internet. Which of the following should you discuss with the customer to educate them while addressing their security concerns? (Select the two best answers.)
explanation: You should discuss firewalls (for the general security of the network) and a VPN (for security while browsing the Internet). These two concepts can help make the home user’s network and laptop more secure and will protect the user’s privacy.
whyWrong: Antimalware helps against malicious programs but does not protect browsing privacy.
A proxy server is a technical tool that a typical home user does not need to discuss.
Advanced TCP/IP settings are too technical to bring up with a typical customer.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – A+ Core 2 (220-1202) Practice Exam, Practice Exam question 48
note: Firewalls and VPNs for a home user are not a single 220-1202 topic; mapped to 2.7 (end-user best practices).

stem: You are part of a security team that is auditing an organization’s server room. You find that a USB drive was previously inserted into three of the servers. There were many login attempts that were successfully performed using common login information. What should you do to prevent the vulnerability from being exploited again? (Select the two best answers.)
explanation: Modify the AutoRun settings for USB drives. Modify AutoPlay/AutoRun by disabling it in the Group Policy Editor or in Settings > Bluetooth & devices > AutoPlay. (Also, the use of USB drives and other removable media should be disabled in the BIOS/UEFI.) Since the login attempt appears to have used common login information, that could indicate that shared credentials might have been compromised and should be changed as well.
whyWrong: Removing admin permissions is vague and would stop administrators from managing the servers.
A software firewall would not stop a local user with a USB drive.
Security updates are important, but they do not fix AutoRun or default credentials.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – A+ Core 2 (220-1202) Practice Exam, Practice Exam question 67

stem: One of your customers has set up a perimeter firewall and has implemented up-to-date antimalware software. The customer asks you what else they can do to improve security. Which of the following will have the greatest impact on their network security? (Select the two best answers.)
options: Assign security rights based on job roles.
explanation: Among other things, you should recommend using strong passwords and assigning security rights based on job roles. Strong passwords are important on routers, wireless devices, switches, computers, and anything else that can be logged in to. Role-based access control means rights and permissions are assigned based on the person’s job in a company—accounting, marketing, and so on.
whyWrong: Daily audits find threats but do not by themselves increase security.
The customer already has up-to-date antimalware, and two antivirus programs can conflict.
Disabling screensavers does not increase security; a password-locked screensaver does.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – A+ Core 2 (220-1202) Practice Exam, Practice Exam question 74
note: Role-based rights follow the principle of least privilege in 220-1202 2.1 (logical security).

stem: Following an overnight network breach, security logs reveal that a dictionary attack successfully breached a single user’s account after 400 attempts. Which of the following measures would be the MOST effective in mitigating this specific threat?
explanation: An account lockout is a security measure typically implemented by computer systems to prevent unauthorized or malicious access to user accounts. If a user enters incorrect login credentials multiple times, their account may be locked out for a certain period of time or until it is manually unlocked by an administrator. This helps protect against dictionary or brute-force attacks, where an attacker repeatedly tries to guess login credentials in order to gain access to an account.
whyWrong: Two-factor authentication helps overall, but lockout is what directly stops repeated guesses.
An IDS can alert on the attack, but no one may be there overnight to respond.
Complex passwords can still be in an attacker's dictionary.
Network segmentation does not stop guesses against one user's account.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 11: Mock Exam: Core 2 (220-1102), Mock Exam question 28
note: 220-1102 2.6 (account management: failed attempts lockout); mapped to 220-1202 2.7 (account management).

stem: When a doctor needs to briefly leave their workstation, which of the following methods is the most effective for quickly securing the workstation?
options: Implementing a key combination to lock the computer upon departure
Verifying the absence of unauthorized individuals in the vicinity
Setting up a screensaver to automatically lock the computer after approximately 30 minutes of inactivity
Powering off the monitor to prevent unauthorized access to displayed information
explanation: Using a key combination to lock the computer when leaving the workstation is the best way for the doctor to quickly secure the workstation. This action immediately restricts access to the computer, ensuring that any sensitive or confidential information remains protected from unauthorized access during the doctor’s absence. Windows Key + L will lock the workstation.
whyWrong: Checking the area does not secure the workstation itself.
A 30-minute screensaver lock leaves the workstation open far too long.
Turning off the monitor hides the screen but leaves the computer unlocked.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 11: Mock Exam: Core 2 (220-1102), Mock Exam question 45
note: 220-1102 2.6; mapped to 220-1202 2.7 (end-user best practices). The book's explanation says police officer; it was changed to doctor to match the stem.

stem: A systems administrator needs to reset a user’s password due to the user forgetting it. After creating the new password, the systems administrator wants to implement additional security measures to protect the user’s account. Which of the following actions should the systems administrator take?
options: Enable password change requirement at the next login
Prohibit the user from changing the password
Set a password with no expiration date
explanation: After resetting the user’s password, enabling the requirement for the user to change the password at the next login adds an extra layer of security. This ensures that the user creates a new password unique to them and helps prevent unauthorized access to the account.
whyWrong: Stopping the user from changing the password keeps a password the administrator knows.
Disabling the account stops the user from working.
A password that never expires is a security risk.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 11: Mock Exam: Core 2 (220-1102), Mock Exam question 47

stem: When configuring a new laptop for an employee who frequently travels, which security practice would be most effective in ensuring data protection?
options: Enforcing quarterly password changes for enhanced security
Enabling hard drive encryption to safeguard sensitive information
Utilizing a physical laptop lock for theft prevention
explanation: In the given scenario, enabling hard drive encryption would be the best security practice. Hard drive encryption ensures that the data stored on the laptop’s hard drive is protected by encrypting it with a strong encryption algorithm. This helps safeguard sensitive information even if the laptop is lost, stolen, or accessed by unauthorized individuals. By encrypting the hard drive, the data remains unreadable and inaccessible without the appropriate encryption key or password.
whyWrong: A PIN helps at login but does not protect the data if the drive is removed.
Quarterly password changes do not protect the data on a lost laptop.
A cable lock helps against theft but does not protect the data on the drive.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 11: Mock Exam: Core 2 (220-1102), Mock Exam question 50

stem: A recent security audit highlighted a high risk of data loss from lost or stolen laptops. To mitigate this risk for Windows laptop users while minimizing the impact on user experience, which of the following measures would be the most effective?
explanation: When there is a risk of data loss from lost or stolen laptops, the best recommendation is to enable full disk encryption. Full disk encryption ensures that even if the laptop falls into unauthorized hands, the data stored on the hard drive remains inaccessible without the encryption key.
whyWrong: Backups keep a copy of the data but do not stop a thief from reading it.
Biometric login does not protect the data on a removed drive.
Tracking software may find the laptop but does not protect the data.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 11: Mock Exam: Core 2 (220-1102), Mock Exam question 54

stem: As a best practice, after a set period of inactivity on a Windows workstation, what should happen?
options: A password-enabled screensaver should automatically start.
The system should log out the user.
explanation: A screensaver should automatically start after a short period of idle time, and that screensaver should require a password before the user can begin the session again. The system should neither shut down nor restart, since work could still be open. For the same reason, the system should not log out the user.
whyWrong: Shutting down the system could lose open work and is not the practice for idle workstations.
Restarting the system could lose open work and does not protect the session.
Logging out the user could close open work; a locked screensaver protects the session instead.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter), Volume 2 – Chapter 6: Securing Operating Systems, Review Questions question 5

stem: What is normally performed when an employee is offboarded?
options: Their user account’s password is reset.
explanation: When an employee is offboarded, their user account is deleted or disabled. A user account is not created, nor is its password reset, during the offboarding process. A user account normally is created during the onboarding process.
whyWrong: Unlocking an account restores access, which is the opposite of what offboarding does.
A user account is created during onboarding, not offboarding.
Resetting the password leaves the account usable, so it does not remove the departed employee's access.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter), Volume 2 – Chapter 6: Securing Operating Systems, Review Questions question 12

stem: Which of the following is the strongest password?
explanation: This1sV#ryS3cure incorporates uppercase and lowercase letters, numbers, and special characters, and it is 16 characters long. That makes it the strongest password of the listed options. |ocrian# has special characters but is missing uppercase letters and numerals—and it is only 8 characters long. Marqu1sD3S0d does not have any special characters. Thisisverysecure is 16 characters long and has 1 capital letter but does not have any numerals or special characters.
whyWrong: This password has special characters but no uppercase letters or numerals and is only 8 characters long.
This password has mixed case and numbers but no special characters.
This password is long but has only one capital letter and no numerals or special characters.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 48: Workstation Best Practices, Cram Quiz question 1

stem: Your boss is concerned that people who have been terminated will come back in the building and attempt to log on to the network using passwords that they used in the past. What should you do to help protect against this? (Select the two BEST answers.)
options: Set up a password length policy.
Immediately disable the accounts of people who have been terminated.
explanation: The best answers are to configure an account lockout threshold and immediately disable the accounts of anyone who has been terminated. A common method is to use the “three strikes and you’re out” rule for account lockout, meaning that a person can attempt to log on three times before the account is locked out. But, more importantly, you should disable (or lock) the accounts of people who have been offboarded or terminated. The other options are all good security options in general but won’t help much with disgruntled former employees who are attempting to get into the system. Also, some type of authentication system should be in place so that these people cannot get access to the building.
whyWrong: A password length policy makes new passwords stronger but does not block a former employee's old account.
Logon time restrictions limit when users log on, but a former employee could still log on during those hours.
Disabling the Guest account is good practice, but it does not stop logons with former employees' accounts.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 48: Workstation Best Practices, Cram Quiz question 2

stem: A customer complains that while he was away at lunch, someone used his computer to send emails to other coworkers without his knowledge. Which of the following should you recommend that the user do?
options: Unplug the network cable before leaving for lunch.
Enable the out-of-office message in email when leaving for lunch.
explanation: Tell the customer to lock the computer (by pressing Windows+L or by using the Start menu) before leaving for lunch. As long as there is a strong password, other coworkers should not be able to access the system. Screensavers by themselves do not secure systems, but a user can enable the password-protected screensaver feature (but should be aware that there is a delay before the screensaver turns on). Unplugging the network cable is not a legitimate answer; plus, it can always be plugged back in. The out-of-office message will reply only to people emailing the user; it won’t stop outgoing emails.
whyWrong: A screensaver by itself does not secure a computer unless it requires a password, and it has a delay.
Unplugging the network cable is not a real fix, because anyone can plug it back in.
An out-of-office message only replies to incoming email; it does not stop someone sending email.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 48: Workstation Best Practices, Cram Quiz question 3

stem: Which of the following BEST describes encryption?
options: Prevents unauthorized users from viewing or reading data
Prevents unauthorized users from deleting data
Prevents unauthorized users from posing as the original source sending data
Prevents unauthorized users from decompressing files
explanation: Encryption prevents unauthorized users from viewing or reading data. Properly configured permissions prevent unauthorized users from deleting data or attempting to decompress files. A strong logon password prevents unauthorized users from posing as the original source sending data.
whyWrong: Properly set permissions, not encryption, stop unauthorized users from deleting data.
A strong logon password, not encryption, stops someone posing as the original sender.
Permissions, not encryption, control whether users can decompress files.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 48: Workstation Best Practices, Cram Quiz question 4

stem: How can you prevent applications from automatically executing and possibly infecting a computer with malware when removable media is inserted?
options: Enable the account lockout threshold policy.
explanation: If you disable AutoPlay, removable media won’t automatically start its AutoRun application (if it has one), and any embedded malware won’t have a chance to infect the system before you scan the media. The account lockout threshold specifies the number of times a user can attempt to log on to Windows before being logged off. BitLocker and BitLocker-To-Go are used for encryption, not for blocking removable media from automatically executing files.
whyWrong: The account lockout threshold limits failed logon attempts; it does not affect removable media.
BitLocker encrypts drives; it does not stop programs from running when media is inserted.
BitLocker-To-Go encrypts removable drives; turning it off does not block automatic execution.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 48: Workstation Best Practices, Cram Quiz question 5

stem: Which of the following account settings is used to limit the time of day a user is allowed to log on to a Windows system?
explanation: Logon Hours allows or disallows certain hours of the day that a user can log on to the network. You configure this setting in the user's Properties dialog box under the Account tab by clicking the Logon Hours button. The Account Lockout Threshold setting is related to the number of unsuccessful logon attempts before an account is locked out. The Account Expiration setting is for setting a date when an account is automatically disabled. User Permissions defines what a user can do on the system (such as read, write, or execute files).
whyWrong: The account lockout threshold sets how many failed logons are allowed before the account locks.
Account expiration sets a date when the account is disabled, not the hours of the day it can be used.
User permissions define what a user can do with files, not when the user can log on.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 48: Workstation Best Practices, Cram Quiz question 6

stem: Which of the following is a built-in credential storage option in macOS?
explanation: macOS utilizes Keychain to store passwords, certificates, and other sensitive information. Credential Manager is the built-in credential storage option for Windows. GNOME Keyring is a keyring service commonly used in Linux distributions using the GNOME GUI, while KWallet is another keyring service used in Linux distributions using KDE.
whyWrong: Credential Manager is the built-in credential store of Windows, not macOS.
GNOME Keyring is a keyring service used in Linux distributions with the GNOME desktop.
KWallet is a keyring service used in Linux distributions with the KDE desktop.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 48: Workstation Best Practices, Cram Quiz question 7
note: Credential stores are not a named 220-1202 2.7 topic; mapped to password considerations.

stem: Which TWO are benefits of disabling unused services on a Windows workstation? (Choose two.)
options: It reduces the attack surface that attackers can exploit
It frees RAM and CPU time for the programs in use
It removes the need to install security updates
It increases the free space on the system drive
explanation: Every running service is code that an attacker might exploit, so turning off the ones not needed shrinks the attack surface. Unused services also use memory and processor time in the background. Disabling them with services.msc can make the system more responsive and start faster.
whyWrong: Security updates are still needed for the OS and the services that stay enabled.
Disabling a service stops it from running but does not delete its files from the drive.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 48: Workstation Best Practices

stem: A senior manager who is attending a conference needs to ensure that confidential data stored on a laptop computer is secured when the laptop is shut down. What will BEST secure the data at rest?
options: Use Pretty Good Privacy (PGP) to encrypt the system files
explanation: BitLocker will protect the data at rest. If the laptop is stolen, then the thief would have to know the BitLocker password. If they enter the wrong password, then the system will lock the attacker out.
whyWrong: Encrypting only the system files with PGP would not protect the confidential data.
Restricting login times only limits when an account can sign in and does not encrypt data.
A timeout or screen lock protects a running session, not the data on a powered-off laptop.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 8: Security, Objective 2.6 question 1

stem: An administrator must ensure that user accounts are added to groups, giving only the necessary privileges needed to carry out assigned tasks. What best practice will ensure that users do not become over-privileged?
options: Ensure all users are members of the Power Users group only
